analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act's individual and small-business tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on February 9, 2022 and sat there until the 117th Congress ended, so the 2017 tax cuts remain scheduled to expire after 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Most of the 2017 tax law's changes to individual taxes — lower rates, a larger standard deduction, a $2,000 child tax credit — are written to expire after 2025. This bill would write them into permanent law instead, along with the 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses, a doubled estate and gift tax exemption, and a higher alternative minimum tax exemption. It would also permanently keep the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions and end miscellaneous itemized deductions for good.
analysis.who_benefits: Most income tax filers keep the lower rates, larger standard deduction, and $2,000-per-child credit they received under the 2017 law instead of seeing them lapse after 2025. The largest dollar gains, though, go to the top: wealthy families get a permanently doubled estate and gift tax exemption, high earners benefit from the raised alternative minimum tax exemption with a phase-out that doesn't start until $1 million, and owners of partnerships, S-corporations, and law or investment firms get the 20% pass-through deduction locked in. Servicemembers, families of students whose loans are discharged on death or disability, people with ABLE accounts, and charities also gain specific permanent benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Most filers, but top earners and estates most

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the lower individual rate brackets, including the 37% top rate and the 12%, 22%, and 24% middle brackets, that are otherwise scheduled to expire after 2025.
Makes permanent the larger standard deduction and the $2,000 child tax credit (up to $1,400 refundable, phasing out above $400,000 for couples and $200,000 for others).
Makes permanent the 20% deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as partnerships, S-corporations, and sole proprietorships.
Doubles the estate and gift tax exemption amount, from a $5 million base to a $10 million base, and makes permanent the higher alternative minimum tax exemption for individuals.

Makes permanent the exclusion of student loan discharges after 2025 due to death or disability from taxable income, the increased contribution limits for ABLE accounts for people with disabilities, the 60%-of-income limit for cash charitable contributions, and the tax exclusion for Sinai Peninsula combat-zone benefits.
Makes permanent the $750,000 limit on deductible mortgage debt and the limitation on personal casualty loss deductions to federally declared disasters.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, since making expiring tax cuts permanent removes the revenue they were scheduled to bring back — roughly $1.5 trillion or more over a decade by independent estimates of the 2017 law's individual provisions. Because the largest provisions (the doubled estate exemption, the alternative minimum tax relief, and the pass-through deduction) flow mainly to high-income households, the lost revenue is skewed toward tax cuts for the top, leaving less room for other spending or requiring more borrowing. Some groups lose relative to current law: the bill permanently repeals the deduction for personal exemptions, permanently ends miscellaneous itemized deductions (which covered things like tax preparation and investment expenses), and locks in the $10,000 state and local tax cap, which hits itemizers in high-tax states hardest. It also repeals the more generous 2021 child tax credit expansion, locking in the less generous 2017 version.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal treasury; some high-tax-state filers

drawbacks.text: The benefits are heavily skewed by income: the doubled estate and gift tax exemption applies only to estates above roughly $12 million per person under current inflation-adjusted levels, the alternative minimum tax phase-out does not begin until $1 million of income, and the pass-through deduction's dollars flow disproportionately to the highest earners — so a large share of the revenue cost buys tax cuts for the wealthiest households while everyone shares the bill.

The bill would permanently lock in the repeal of the personal exemption deduction and miscellaneous itemized deductions, which taken alone raised many larger families' taxes under the 2017 law, and it would permanently deny itemizers any deduction for state and local taxes above $10,000.

It explicitly repeals the provisions of the 2021 child tax credit expansion, settling on the smaller $2,000 credit with only $1,400 refundable rather than the fully refundable credit families received in 2021.

Making expiring tax cuts permanent is a major revenue loss; the individual provisions of the 2017 law were scored by independent estimators at well over a trillion dollars a decade when extended, increasing deficits or requiring offsetting cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most working families, the bill preserves real tax cuts — lower rates, a bigger standard deduction, a $2,000-per-child credit — that would otherwise end after 2025, which is genuinely valuable. The honest problem is the price tag and the tilt: the most expensive pieces (the doubled estate exemption, the alternative minimum tax exemption for million-dollar incomes, and the permanent pass-through deduction) go almost entirely to the top of the income distribution, and the whole package adds to deficits. Families also give up the more generous 2021 child credit design permanently. On net, it is a broad tax cut whose dollar weight sits with wealthy households and business owners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened before the 117th Congress ended, so the bill died in committee.

narrative.text: Rodney Davis (R-IL) introduced the bill on February 9, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
111 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action, and the full House never considered the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Because the bill died, the individual provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act remain scheduled to expire at the end of 2025, as the CRS summary describes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No taxpayer's bill changed as a result — the bill never moved. What survived was the status quo: the scheduled 2025 expiration of the 2017 tax cuts stayed on the books, and the Ways and Means Committee and House leadership avoided taking a recorded position on extending cuts whose cost is concentrated at the top.

for.name: Rep. Rodney Davis
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual and pass-through provisions permanent.

for.name: 111 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Ways and Means members such as Kevin Brady and Jackie Walorski.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill; it sat with no action after referral.

against.name: Rep. Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the chamber never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — all 111 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on — and the Democratic majority took no action on it.

industries.note: A doubled estate and gift tax exemption ($10 million base, indexed to roughly double today's level) and a permanently higher alternative minimum tax exemption with no phase-out until $1 million of income deliver the largest dollar benefits in the bill to the top of the income distribution; the cost is revenue the public otherwise would collect.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S-corporations, law, investment, and real estate firms)
industries.note: The bill permanently locks in the 20% deduction for qualified business income, making it a permanent feature of the tax code rather than a provision expiring in 2025; independent analyses of the deduction show its dollars concentrate among the highest-earning business owners.

Making the $10,000 state and local tax cap and the $750,000 mortgage-interest cap permanent keeps deductions limited for affluent itemizers in states like New York, California, and New Jersey, while ending the scheduled 2025 change benefits the cap's original defenders.
The bill makes permanent the higher 60%-of-income limit on deductible cash contributions, which encourages large gifts to charities.

industries.industry: Families of student loan borrowers, people with disabilities (ABLE accounts), and servicemembers
industries.note: Permanent tax-free treatment of student loans discharged on death or disability, increased ABLE account contribution limits, and tax-exempt Sinai combat-zone benefits are narrow, concrete gains for these groups.
